## Meet Yesica
For residents on Harrison Street, the leptospirosis alert was not only about disease...

html:
For many people living along Harrison Street, daily life already involves uncertainty. Now, concerns about disease are adding a new layer of fear.

Following a public health alert warning about the risk of leptospirosis — a bacterial disease linked to rat activity and contaminated water — residents say the threat feels both invisible and unavoidable.

“I see rats every night,” said one resident who has lived in the area for months. “When it rains, the water runs everywhere. You don’t know what’s in it.”

Leptospirosis spreads when bacteria carried in rat urine contaminate soil and standing water. The bacteria can enter the human body through small cuts, wounds, or mucous membranes such as the eyes, nose, or mouth.

But for residents living outdoors, avoiding contaminated environments is not always possible.

After rainfall, puddles often form along sidewalks and near sleeping areas. Residents say water collects in low-lying spaces, soaking belongings and creating conditions that feel unsafe.

“When it rains, everything gets wet — your shoes, your clothes, where you sleep,” another resident said. “You don’t have a choice but to step in it.”

Public health officials say moisture plays a major role in spreading bacteria. Rainwater can carry contamination through soil and drains, increasing exposure risks for anyone walking through wet areas.

For residents without access to consistent sanitation, even minor injuries — small cuts or scrapes — can become potential entry points for infection.

Many say they worry about how easily exposure could happen.

“You don’t always know when you have a cut,” one resident said. “You just hope you don’t get sick.”

Health officials warn that symptoms of leptospirosis can resemble everyday illnesses, making early detection difficult.

Common symptoms include fever, chills, headaches, and muscle aches — signs that can easily be mistaken for flu or exhaustion.

That uncertainty creates anxiety among residents who already face barriers to healthcare access.

“If I feel sick, how do I know if it’s serious?” one resident asked. “Sometimes you just push through because there’s nowhere to rest.”

Community advocates say this uncertainty contributes to fear spreading alongside the disease risk itself.

“When people don’t have clear access to healthcare or safe shelter, even a preventable disease becomes a major threat,” said a local outreach volunteer familiar with the area.

Residents say rodent activity has been a long-standing issue, but recent health warnings have made the problem feel more urgent.

Trash accumulation, limited waste disposal, and standing water create conditions where rodents thrive. Many residents believe those conditions increase the likelihood of infection.

“You can hear them moving at night,” said one resident. “You try to keep things clean, but there’s only so much you can do.”

Public health guidance recommends avoiding standing water and covering open wounds. But residents say those recommendations are difficult to follow without stable infrastructure.

“People are being told what to avoid,” said a community volunteer. “But they’re living in conditions where avoiding exposure isn’t realistic.”

For many in the community, the greatest concern is not just the disease itself, but what it represents — another reminder of vulnerability.

Residents say they want clearer communication about risks, prevention steps, and available resources.

“We just want to know what’s happening and how to stay safe,” one resident said.

Advocates emphasize that disease risk in vulnerable communities is often tied to environmental conditions beyond individual control.

“When people lack safe housing and sanitation, public health risks grow,” said a volunteer working in the area. “This isn’t just about bacteria. It’s about living conditions.”

Community members say their concerns extend beyond immediate health risks to long-term safety.

They want better sanitation access, rodent control, and clearer public health outreach — measures they believe could reduce both exposure and anxiety.

“People shouldn’t have to worry about getting sick just from walking outside,” one resident said.

As rainfall continues and environmental conditions remain challenging, residents say their biggest fear is uncertainty — not knowing when or where exposure might happen.

For many, the risk of disease is no longer theoretical.

It is part of everyday life.
